title: Shared Data & the Database-per-Service Problem
summary: Why a shared database quietly defeats the point of microservices, and how to query and stay in sync across services once data is split.

slides.markdown:
The single most common way microservices quietly become a [service-decomposition](service-decomposition) failure — a distributed monolith — is a shared database. Splitting the code but not the data means every schema change still needs every team's sign-off.

**Database-per-service** fixes that, but creates a new problem: once data lives in separate databases, you can no longer just `JOIN` across it. This topic covers both halves — why to split, and how to live with the split.

slides.sectionTitle: Database-per-service: why sharing one DB defeats the point of microservices
slides.markdown:
If Orders, Inventory, and Payments all read and write the same database, they are not independent, no matter how separate their codebases and deployments look. Any team can change a column that another team's queries depend on, and no compiler or API contract will catch it — it breaks silently in production.

**Database-per-service** means each service owns its schema exclusively; every other service reaches its data only through the owning service's API, never directly against its tables. This restores the two things microservices are supposed to buy: independent deployability (no cross-team schema coordination) and failure isolation (one service's database being slow doesn't directly slow a query running against another).

The cost is real too — you give up cheap, consistent cross-entity `JOIN`s, which is exactly what the rest of this topic addresses.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: shared DB anti-pattern vs database-per-service
slides.markdown:
![Shared database anti-pattern vs database-per-service with API-only calls](assets/database-per-service.svg)

In the anti-pattern, every service can read and write every table, so a schema change anywhere risks breaking code everywhere. In database-per-service, the only sanctioned path between services' data is a call through the owning service's API.

That single rule — no direct cross-service table access, ever — is what the rest of this topic exists to help you keep without breaking your ability to query across services.

slides.sectionTitle: Querying across services once the data is split: API composition and CQRS
slides.markdown:
Once data is split, "show me all orders with the customer's name and current loyalty tier" can no longer be one query. Two common answers.

**API composition**: the caller (or a dedicated aggregator service) calls Orders for the order list, then calls Customers for each customer's name and tier, and stitches the results together in application code. Simple, but N+1 calls and multiple round trips can get slow for large result sets.

**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): maintain a separate, denormalized read model — built ahead of time from events published by Orders and Customers — that already has order-plus-customer data joined and ready to query directly. Writes still go to each service's own database; reads hit the pre-built view.

API composition is simpler and fine for low-volume, few-service queries; CQRS pays off once a query needs to be fast and spans data owned by many services.

slides.sectionTitle: Keeping data in sync across services: events and CDC
slides.markdown:
A CQRS read model (or any service that keeps its own copy of another service's data) needs to stay updated when the source changes. Two common mechanisms. **Domain events**: the owning service explicitly publishes an event — `OrderPlaced`, `CustomerTierChanged` — whenever something relevant happens, and interested services subscribe and update their own copies.

**Change Data Capture (CDC)**: instead of the service remembering to publish events, a tool (like Debezium) tails the source database's write-ahead log and turns every row change into an event automatically — useful when you can't easily add publish calls to existing code, but it couples a downstream consumer to the source's schema more tightly than a deliberate domain event would.

Either way, the receiving side ends up **eventually consistent** with the source — there's a lag, usually milliseconds to seconds, during which the copy is stale.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: shared DB vs database-per-service on consistency and autonomy
slides.markdown:
| | Shared database | Database-per-service |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-entity queries | Trivial — a single `JOIN` | Requires API composition or a CQRS read model |
| Consistency | Strong — one transaction, one commit | Eventual — copies sync via events, with lag |
| Team autonomy | Low — any schema change risks breaking another team's queries | High — each team owns and evolves its schema freely |
| Failure isolation | Weak — one runaway query can slow every service | Strong — one database being slow doesn't touch another's |

**How to decide:** if you need strong, immediate consistency across entities and only one team owns them all, a shared schema (even within one service) is fine; once multiple teams need independent schema evolution, pay the eventual-consistency cost of splitting the data.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: two services silently sharing a table "just for now"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We'll let the new Shipping service read directly from the Orders table temporarily, just to ship faster — we'll fix it later."

**Why it's wrong:** "temporarily" rarely gets revisited once it works, and every day it exists, Orders can't change that table's schema without checking whether Shipping's queries still work — the exact cross-team coupling database-per-service was meant to eliminate. The workaround becomes permanent because removing it requires coordinated work with no urgent forcing function.

**Correct model:** if Shipping needs order data, give it a real API call (or an event feed) from day one, even if it's slower to build than a direct query — the schema-coupling cost compounds silently, while the API's cost is paid once, up front.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: CDC replication lag and when it becomes visible inconsistency
slides.subTitle: Estimation
slides.markdown:
Change Data Capture (CDC) keeping two services' data in sync has a concrete failure mode worth naming: **replication lag turning into visible inconsistency**. If a CDC pipeline (reading a database's write-ahead log and publishing change events, e.g. via Debezium into Kafka) normally lags by a few hundred milliseconds to a couple seconds, a downstream consumer that's briefly behind (a deploy, a slow consumer group) can show data a customer already knows is stale — a customer who just updated their address sees the old one on a different screen for as long as that lag lasts.

Concrete example: an order service updates its own database instantly, but the shipping service's CDC-synced copy of the customer's address lags by 2 seconds under normal load — with a consumer restart, that lag can spike to 30-60 seconds while the consumer group catches up on a backlog, and any shipping label generated in that window uses the stale address.

The takeaway: CDC gives you eventual consistency with a lag you should measure and monitor directly (consumer group lag is a standard Kafka metric) — treating it as instantaneous just because it's "usually fast" is how stale-data bugs make it to production.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: the dual-write window when extracting a service's data
slides.markdown:
Extracting a service out of a shared database is where the database-per-service goal actually gets tested, and the dangerous window is the **dual-write period**: while both the old shared table and the new service's own database are being written to, in parallel, to keep the migration safe to roll back.

Concrete example: splitting a "users" table out of a monolith into its own service means, for some transition period, writes go to both the old table (still read by other parts of the monolith that haven't migrated yet) and the new service's database — any bug in that dual-write logic (a write that succeeds in one but fails in the other) silently diverges the two copies, and the divergence is often invisible until a customer notices stale data days later. Teams commonly run a reconciliation job during this window, comparing both copies on a schedule and alerting on drift, specifically because dual-write bugs are quiet failures.

**Testing:** whether you plan for the dual-write window as a real risk period with its own monitoring, rather than treating "extract the service" as a single atomic step.
